progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: chem-m7-c03 (shapes: trigonal planar C=C carbons, tetrahedral single-bonded carbons; the double bond's second bond is weaker and lies above and below the carbons; general formulas; saturated and unsaturated), chem-m7-c01 (naming hydrocarbons, locants, di-), chem-m7-c02 (structural isomers; "-ol" means an O–H group and the number says which carbon; cyclobutane; but-1-ene and cyclobutane both C₄H₈). Module 5: a catalyst speeds up a reaction and is not used up (chem-m5-c04b); raising the pressure shifts a gas equilibrium towards fewer gas molecules (chem-m5-c04a). Year 11: balancing equations. Not assumed: addition reaction, reagent, hydrogenation, halogenation, hydration, haloalkane naming.
progression.startsWith: Compare saturated and unsaturated bonds. The video opens: Vegetable oil is a liquid, and its long molecules contain carbon to carbon double bonds. Add hydrogen gas, with a nickel catalyst and heat, and the hydrogen adds across some of those double bonds. The oil turns into a soft solid.
progression.stopsAfter: explaining why an alkene can add and an alkane cannot; writing equations with structural formulas and conditions on the arrow for an alkene with H₂, X₂, HX and H₂O; naming the haloalkane and alcohol products; recognising when an unsymmetrical alkene gives two possible products. No alkane substitution or alkyne addition (chem-m7-c04b), no test method or limits (chem-m7-p02), no Markovnikov's rule.
progression.nextLesson: why alkanes substitute while alkenes and alkynes add (route chem-m7-c04, delivery part c04b).

teaching.task: Hydrogen can add across the double bonds in vegetable oil and turn it solid. What else can add across a C=C bond, under what conditions, and what product does each make?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) hydrogen can add to the double bonds in vegetable oil (1); (2) alkanes have no spare bond; an alkene's weaker, exposed second bond can break, leaving one spare bond on each carbon (2); (3) addition: two molecules make one, the reagent splits one piece to each carbon, and those carbons become tetrahedral (3); (4) hydrogen needs a catalyst and heat, and the catalyst is not used up, so it goes on the arrow (4); (5) halogens add at room temperature; halogen naming; the bromine is used up, so bromine water loses its colour (5); (6) a hydrogen halide splits into two different pieces (6); (7) water needs a catalyst, heat and pressure, and pressure helps because two gas molecules become one (7); (8) different pieces on an unsymmetrical alkene can land either way round, so two possible products (8); (9) the equation check: one product, nothing lost (9); memory aid (10); two attempts and brief feedback (11 to 14); handoff (15); key notes (16).
teaching.conversationalApproach: hydrogen added across the double bonds in vegetable oil turns it into a soft solid, so the video asks what else can add across a C=C bond, under what conditions and what product each makes. An alkane is saturated with no spare bond, while an alkene's weaker second bond can open and give each carbon a spare bond, so addition is two molecules making one with nothing lost: the reagent splits and one piece goes on each carbon, which turns flat carbons tetrahedral. The four reagents follow one at a time, each with its conditions on the arrow: hydrogen with a nickel catalyst and heat, halogens at room temperature (named with a locant like a branch, and bromine water losing its colour), hydrogen halides putting H and X on different carbons, and water as steam with a phosphoric acid catalyst and high pressure because the equilibrium shifts towards fewer gas molecules. An unsymmetrical alkene such as propene gives two possible products and an answer writes both, and every addition equation is checked by counting atoms, with HBr as a second product marking substitution instead. The memory aid is split the reagent, one piece on each carbon, then match the conditions. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: Vegetable oil is a liquid, and its long molecules contain carbon to carbon double bonds. Add hydrogen gas, with a nickel catalyst and heat, and the hydrogen adds across some of those double bonds. The oil turns into a soft solid. For much of the last century, that's how margarine was made. Hydrogen isn't the only thing that can add to a double bond, though. So what can add across a C double bond C, and what does it make?
teaching.understandingCheck: (A1) "Propene reacts with chlorine at room temperature. Write a balanced equation for this reaction using structural formulae, and name the organic product." New reagent and alkene pairing for students (scenes use ethene with bromine); tests the one-piece-each pattern, an unsymmetrical alkene with a symmetrical reagent (one product) and halogen naming with locants. Crossed mistake: "CH₂=CHCH₂Cl + HCl" (a substitution written for an addition, with HCl as a second product; site lesson 5 Common Error). (A2) "Compound X has the molecular formula C₄H₈. X decolourises bromine water rapidly. When X reacts with steam in the presence of a phosphoric acid catalyst at high temperature and pressure, only one alcohol product is possible. Identify compound X. Justify your answer." Site worked example 3 rebuilt with the evidence corrected (correction 1). Tests the C=C evidence, chem-m7-c02's C₄H₈ isomers and the symmetrical against unsymmetrical idea (scene 8). Crossed mistake: "but-1-ene" (the site's answer).
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017), as printed: "investigate, write equations and construct models to represent the reactions of unsaturated hydrocarbons when added to a range of chemicals, including but not limited to:; hydrogen (H2); halogens (X2); hydrogen halides (HX); water (H2O) (ACSCH136)" This part covers alkenes with all four listed reagents. Alkyne addition (the other unsaturated hydrocarbons) is chem-m7-c04b. this video starts by comparing saturated and unsaturated bonds and stops at predicting the products and conditions of alkene addition with H₂, X₂, HX and H₂O. It teaches: an alkane's carbons already have four single bonds, so nothing can add (saturated); an alkene's double bond has a weaker second bond whose electrons are exposed above and below the carbons (chem-m7-c03 callback), so it can break and each carbon gains one new bond; an addition reaction (two reactants make one product, no atoms lost; the reagent splits, one piece to each carbon of the old double bond; those carbons change from trigonal planar to tetrahedral), shown with one ink ball-and-stick model; hydrogenation (ethene to ethane; nickel catalyst, about 150 °C; the catalyst on the arrow, Module 5 callback; margarine context); halogenation (ethene to 1,2-dibromoethane; room temperature, no catalyst; halogens named as prefixes with locants; bromine water loses its orange colour, with the test itself left to the practical); hydrohalogenation (ethene to bromoethane; room temperature, no catalyst); hydration (ethene to ethanol; steam, phosphoric acid catalyst, about 300 °C, high pressure; why high pressure helps, Module 5 callback); unsymmetrical alkenes (propene) give two possible products with HX or water, symmetrical ones (but-2-ene) give one; checking an addition equation (one product, every reagent atom on the old double-bond carbons; HBr as a by-product would be substitution). Not here: alkane substitution with UV light, alkyne addition and why alkanes substitute (chem-m7-c04b, the next video; one handoff sentence and one forward line in scene 3); the bromine water test method, observations and its limits (chem-m7-p02); which of two products forms more (Markovnikov's rule, not required by the 2017 syllabus; author note b); combustion (site lesson 5 card 2; alcohol combustion in chem-m7-c07); addition polymerisation (site lesson 5 card 5; chem-m7-c14); fermentation against hydration (chem-m7-c06); dehydration of alcohols (chem-m7-c08a); haloalkane substitution reactions (chem-m7-c13); reaction mechanisms; cis and trans products.

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer. Colour key as chem-m7-c01 and c03: carbon skeleton ink; hydrogens soft grey; the C=C teal, its second bond shown as a teal cloud above and below the axis; bromine deep orange-brown; chlorine green; oxygen red-brown; new atoms from the reagent keep their colour in the product; condition chips navy on the arrow. Board layout (constant): top-left the reagent chip ("Reagent 1 of 4: H₂"); centre the equation stage strip, one equation at a time; the conditions card small at the right from scene 4 on; plates small at the left or right only in scenes 1, 4, 5, 7 and 14. Clutter rule: at most three text items bright at once; every label fades when its sentence ends; the previous equation leaves before the next one draws. Reuse: painted plates (inspected 21 Oct): `m7-bromine-water-orange-v1.png` (a clear test tube about half full of bright orange liquid, no stopper, no label, no person or hand; 2000 × 2000) and `m7-bromine-water-colourless-v1.png` (the matching tube with colourless liquid at the same level; 2000 × 2000), shown in place of each other as a before and after in scene 5; `m7-bromine-water-pair-v1.png` (the two tubes side by side; 2000 × 2000) in attempt 2's feedback; `m7-ethanol-fuel-bottle-v1.png` (an amber stoppered bottle, half full of pale liquid, no label; 2000 × 2000) small in scene 7. All scale uniformly only, never stretched. New plates: `m7-vegetable-oil-bottle-v1.png` and `m7-margarine-tub-v1.png` (hook, scene 4); see Assets. No human figures.

On "but-two-ene" "Identify compound X" is underlined; answer chip "X = but-2-ene, CH₃CH=CHCH₃ (gives only butan-2-ol)". On "doesn't fit" a chip "X = but-1-ene" fades in and is crossed (caption "unsymmetrical: two possible alcohols"). Hold about 1 second. Hold about 1 second.
